title: THE BIG PICTURE
headline: WHERE WAS CRIME REPORTED?
paragraphs: In 2016, 125,790 criminal offences were reported across Nigeria’s 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory.
But the national total hides a much more uneven geography.
Lagos alone accounted for 45,385 reported offences, more than one-third of all cases recorded nationally.
The Federal Capital Territory followed with 13,181, while Delta recorded 7,867.
Together, these three areas accounted for more than half of all reported offences in the dataset.
instruction: Hover over a state to explore the numbers.

title: POPULATION
headline: THE DENOMINATOR CHANGES THE STORY
paragraphs: A large population creates more opportunities for offences to be reported, so comparing states by total cases alone can obscure differences in scale.
Rates allow us to ask a different question:
How many reported offences were recorded relative to the size of the population?
The geography shifts when population enters the equation.
This does not make one measure "correct" and the other "wrong."

title: CONCENTRATION
headline: THREE PLACES DOMINATE THE COUNT
paragraphs: Lagos, the Federal Capital Territory and Delta together account for more than half of all reported offences in the dataset.
But concentration in the raw count does not automatically mean these places had the highest rate of reported offences.

title: FOUR CATEGORIES
headline: FOUR CRIMES.
paragraphs: The national total is made up of four broad offence categories.
The geography changes when the definition of crime changes.
Allow the reader to switch between the four categories.

title: PERSONS
headline: CRIMES AGAINST PERSONS
paragraphs: 45,554 reported offences in the national dataset were classified as offences against persons.
The category includes crimes involving human beings, including murder, manslaughter, infanticide, concealment of birth, rape and physical abuse.
Use the established crime-red visual language.

title: PROPERTY
headline: PROPERTY OFFENCES DOMINATE THE NATIONAL TOTAL
paragraphs: 65,397 reported offences were classified as offences against property.
That represents 52.0% of the national total.
The category includes offences involving belongings and property, including stealing, receiving stolen property, false pretence, robbery, burglary and housebreaking.
Use orange as the category signal.

title: LAWFUL AUTHORITY
headline: OFFENCES AGAINST LAWFUL AUTHORITY
paragraphs: 12,144 reported offences were classified as offences against lawful authority.
These include offences against establishments of law, such as tax-related offences.

title: LOCAL ACTS
headline: LOCAL ACTS
paragraphs: 2,695 reported offences were classified as offences against local acts.
These refer to offences against laws that cannot be enforced outside Nigeria, including legislation such as the Liquor Act or Firearms Act.

title: STATE SIGNATURES
headline: EVERY STATE HAS A DIFFERENT SIGNATURE
paragraphs: The national profile is useful, but it can hide how different individual states are.

title: DIVERGENCE
headline: WHERE STATES DEPART FROM THE NATIONAL PROFILE
paragraphs: Property offences represented 52.0% of reported offences nationally.
But individual states do not necessarily follow that pattern.
This map shows how far each state's property share differs from the national 52.0% benchmark.
More property-heavy than the national profile.
Less property-heavy than the national profile.
Use the established diverging color scale.
Do not describe a state as "better" or "worse."
This is a difference in composition, not a safety ranking.

title: THERE IS NO SINGLE MAP
headline: THERE IS NO SINGLE MAP OF CRIME
paragraphs: Raw counts tell us where the most offences were reported.
Rates tell us where reported offences were highest relative to population.
Crime categories reveal different spatial patterns.
The map changes because the question changes.
Allow the reader to move between:
The geography of reported crime is not one map.
It is a collection of different patterns revealed by the question we choose to ask.

title: LIMITATIONS
headline: A MAP OF REPORTED CRIME IS NOT A MAP OF ALL CRIME.
paragraphs: These data represent reported offences recorded in the 2016 dataset.
They do not capture every offence that occurred.
Differences in reporting behaviour, policing, access to authorities, recording practices and other factors may influence the observed geography.
Therefore, a high number of reported offences should not automatically be interpreted as proof that a place was more dangerous, nor should a low number be interpreted as proof that it was safer.
The maps describe the geography of reported offences.
They do not provide a complete measure of public safety.
